title: When Context Gets Root: Privilege Escalation in LLM Harnesses

object.carrier: harness context-reconstruction surfaces that persist or re-inject attacker-controlled tool-level content: delegated subagent user messages; persistent goals (resent as user-level prompts); scheduled tasks (cron-like future user-level prompts); installed custom-subagent configuration plus AGENTS.md loaded at harness restart; skill metadata (system-effective) and invoked skill bodies (user-level)

safety_property.statement: Instruction privilege granted by message role labels must reflect true provenance: tool-level (untrusted) content must never be presented at user or system-effective level, and attacker-derived text must never be interpreted as user authorization by the permission reviewer. The property fails whenever harness context reconstruction (delegation, persistent goals, scheduled tasks, custom-subagent installation, skill installation) relabels content without preserving provenance; it is judged by whether attacker-induced security-sensitive actions are proposed by the working agent and allowed by Auto PR.
safety_property.operationalized_as: 13 attack objectives spanning confidentiality, integrity, availability, and RCE executed on six coding-agent harnesses under full-access execution and automatic permission review; success measured as objectives achieved (x/13), post-escalation success, installation success rate, and per-attempt attack success rate

capabilities: controls workspace artifacts the agent may read (repository files, task documents) and any state the agent derives from them
chooses text and code in those artifacts to induce normal harness operations: delegation, goal creation, task scheduling, custom-subagent installation
knows the victim harness design and its context-construction behavior
assumptions: all victim components (harness, working model, reviewer model) are uncompromised and behave exactly as configured and trained
attacker content first enters the model at the tool level through a file-reading or search tool
every attack originates at the tool level; malicious behavior remains visible to the model (plain-text Python, no obfuscation)
evaluation caps each case at 10 attempts (10 attempts per method for baselines)
not_covered: direct injection of higher-privilege context (e.g., auto-loaded subagents or skills)
attacker control of user request, harness, working/reviewer models, developer instructions, tool permissions, sandbox policy, or approval policy
initial shell access or execution capability outside the victim agent
prompt injection or model jailbreaks, user deception, and obtaining genuine authorization
obfuscated attacks that hide malicious behavior from the model (Friendly Fire style)

intervention.name: Instruction privilege escalation (attack): tool-to-user and tool-to-system escalation via agent-side context reconstruction
intervention.description: Normal harness context-construction operations (multi-agent delegation, persistent goals, scheduled tasks, custom-subagent installation, skill installation) carry attacker-controlled tool-level content into new model-facing contexts at a higher instruction level (user message or system-effective prompt), dropping its original provenance. The elevated content then directs the working agent and is read by automatic permission review as user authorization.

results.claim: In the paper's evaluation, delegation-based tool-to-user escalation achieves all 13 attack objectives on every harness under full-access execution and on all three harnesses that provide Auto PR (Claude Code, Codex, Qwen Code) under automatic permission review, with per-attempt attack success rates of 31.7%-100% and over 86% success once escalation occurs.
results.metric: objectives achieved and attack success rate (ASR)
results.setting: six coding-agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Kimi, OpenCode) under full-access execution and Auto PR; attacker controls repository content; each case capped at 10 attempts
results.quote: Overall, tool-to-user escalation achieves all 13 attack objectives, with attack success rates ranging from 31.7% to 100%. Once escalated, the attack succeeds in over 86% of cases.

denominator.n_total: all execution attempts per objective (each case capped at 10 attempts)
denominator.how_counted: Table 7: attack success is measured over all execution attempts; post-escalation success is conditional on escalation

results.claim: Across the evaluated harness-permission configurations, tool-to-user escalation yields a 97.3% mean success rate after escalation and tool-to-system escalation an 80.3% mean per-attempt attack success rate.
results.metric: mean post-escalation success rate / mean per-attempt ASR
results.setting: six coding-agent harnesses, 13 attack objectives, full-access and Auto PR regimes
results.quote: Across the evaluated harness–permission configurations, tool-to-user escalation achieves a 97.3% mean success rate after escalation, while tool-to-system escalation achieves an 80.3% mean per-attempt attack success rate.

denominator.n_total: the 6 Full Access + 3 Auto PR harness-permission rows of Table 7 and Table 10 (9 configurations)
denominator.how_counted: Both figures are means across the evaluated harness-permission configurations: 97.3% is the mean of the 'Success after escalation' column of Table 7 (Full Access: 100.0/100.0/96.2/100.0/96.2/96.2; Auto PR: 86.7/100.0/100.0) and 80.3% is the mean of the 'Attack success rate' column of Table 10 (Full Access: 86.7/100.0/86.7/65.0/86.7/86.7; Auto PR: 76.5/72.2/61.9, using the Table 10 value 72.2% for Codex although the prose states 70.0%). All nine per-configuration cell values are verbatim in the tables and both means reproduce the stated 97.3% and 80.3%.

results.claim: Tool-level baseline attacks (MCPTox, CoT Forgery, ChatInject) achieve 0 of 13 objectives on all three Auto PR harnesses, whereas escalation succeeds on all objectives under the same regime.
results.value: 0/13 objectives for each baseline method under Auto PR
results.comparison: 0/13 baseline vs 13/13 escalation under Auto PR
results.setting: Claude Code, Codex, Qwen Code under automatic permission review; attack prompt in README.md targeting setup.py; 10 attempts per method
results.quote:
| Automatic Permission Review |
| Claude Code | 0/13 | 0/13 | 0/13 |
| Codex | 0/13 | 0/13 | 0/13 |
| Qwen Code | 0/13 | 0/13 | 0/13 |

denominator.how_counted: Each entry reports the number of attack objectives achieved out of 13

results.claim: Tool-to-system escalation via custom-subagent installation achieves high installation success on all six harnesses: 46.2%-100% of trials under Auto PR and 84.6%-100% under full access.
results.value: 46.2%-100% under Auto PR; 84.6%-100% under full access
results.setting: custom subagent installed via tool-to-user escalation; Auto PR when available (Claude Code, Codex, Qwen Code), full access otherwise (Gemini CLI, Kimi, OpenCode)
results.quote: Table 9 shows that tool-to-system escalation achieves high installation success rates. Under Auto PR, Claude Code, Codex, and Qwen Code succeed in 46.2%–100% of trials. Under full-access mode, Gemini CLI, Kimi, and OpenCode succeed in 84.6%–100% of trials.

results.claim: With the malicious payload hidden in a separate script, tool-to-system escalation reaches a 65.0%-100% per-attempt attack success rate on all six harnesses in full-access mode; per Table 10, Codex reaches 100.0% while Claude Code reaches 86.7% (13/15), so the prose statement that 'Claude Code and Codex reaching 100%' conflicts with Table 10.
results.setting: hidden-script custom-subagent variant; six harnesses under full-access execution; attacks detector-confirmed
results.quote: Table 10 reports the attack success rate of the hidden-script variant. In full-access mode, all six harnesses achieve high success rates, ranging from 65.0% to 100%, with Claude Code and Codex reaching 100%.

denominator.n_total: total number of attempts per harness (13-20 in Table 10)
denominator.n_valid: 13 detector-confirmed successful attacks on each harness
denominator.how_counted: Attack success rate is the number of detector-confirmed successful attacks divided by the total number of attempts

results.claim: The hidden-script tool-to-system attack stays effective under automatic permission review, reaching 76.5% on Claude Code, 70.0% on Codex, and 61.9% on Qwen Code; note the prose value for Codex differs from the 72.2% shown in Table 10.
results.metric: attack success rate (ASR) under Auto PR
results.setting: hidden-script custom-subagent variant under automatic permission review; reviewer sees the modifications but approves execution
results.quote: The attack remains effective under Auto PR, reaching 76.5% on Claude Code, 70.0% on Codex, and 61.9% on Qwen Code.

denominator.n_total: attempts per harness under Auto PR (17 / 18 / 21 in Table 10)
denominator.n_valid: 13 detector-confirmed successful attacks on each harness
denominator.how_counted: Attack success rate is the number of detector-confirmed successful attacks divided by the total number of attempts

results.claim: When the malicious intent is stated directly in the system-effective prompt, tool-to-system escalation completes only 55 of 117 objective-configuration combinations, so concealment of the payload matters for this path.
results.setting: direct variant of custom-subagent system prompt; 13 objectives across six harnesses in full-access mode and three under Auto PR
results.quote: when the malicious intent is exposed directly in the system prompt, tool-to-system escalation completes 55 of 117 objective–configuration combinations, covering 13 objectives across six harnesses in full-access mode and three under Auto PR.

denominator.how_counted: 13 objectives across six harnesses in full-access mode and three under Auto PR

results.claim: Tool-to-user escalation through persistent goals and scheduled tasks achieves all 13 attack objectives on all four evaluated agent-accessible paths, showing the vulnerability generalizes beyond multi-agent delegation.
results.value: 13/13 objectives on all four goal and scheduled-task paths
results.setting: four agent-accessible goal/scheduled-task paths in Claude Code, Codex, and Qwen Code; Auto PR when the reconstructed task is visible to the reviewer, full access otherwise
results.quote: Table 12 shows that all four paths achieve all 13 attack objectives. This demonstrates that instruction privilege escalation is not specific to multi-agent delegation, but generalizes across multiple context-reconstruction mechanisms, including persistent goals and scheduled tasks.

denominator.how_counted: all four paths achieve all 13 attack objectives

limitations.statement: The unified system-effective level is only an analytical category, not a single instruction level with uniform privilege; privilege can differ within it across protocols and prompt positions.
